findings.impact: Every published release ISO contains a live control-plane join/registration token and, when set, a GitHub upload token. Anyone who downloads the public ISO can extract live/private/*.conf from the squashfs and authenticate to the control plane (registration/operator bearer) or reuse the upload token, and the token does not expire on its own.
findings.recommendation: Stop baking long-lived tokens into the image. Ship a one-time enrollment token (or per-stick credential generated on first boot and exchanged for a short-lived key), inject BENCH_AGENT_CONF at runtime from a mounted config, and add an automatic rotation/deletion step for the build secret after the release. At minimum, gate ISO publishing on a truncated/least-privilege token and document a mandatory rotation on every public release.

findings.title: CI ISO build runs a --privileged container with the host repository bind-mounted read-write
evidence: live/ci-build.sh:57-62 - 'docker run --rm --privileged -v "$REPO:/work" -w /work -v "$WORKROOT:/bigwork" ... archlinux:latest'
live/ci-build.sh:74-85 - the container re-points host symlinks (.venv, live/out-<gpu>) inside the bind-mounted repo, i.e. it writes to the host checkout
live/ci-build.sh:71 - pacman -Sy runs inside the container pulling arbitrary repo packages

.github/workflows/build-iso.yml:30-32,53 - runner_labels is operator-selectable and can target a self-hosted runner (comment: 'ubuntu-latest = free for public repos' implies self-hosted is also supported)
findings.impact: A --privileged container shares the host kernel, devices and (in practice) can escape to host root. Because the whole repository is mounted read-write and the build executes repo-supplied scripts (pacman/PKGBUILD/mkarchiso) as root, a compromised dependency or malicious commit gets effective root on the runner; on a self-hosted runner that is the persistent lab builder. The container also mutates the host checkout (symlink re-points).
findings.recommendation: Drop --privileged; grant only the capabilities actually needed (CAP_SYS_ADMIN + loop/mount for mkarchiso) and use a scoped /dev/loop* passthrough, or run the build on the dedicated Arch runner (build_native path) exclusively. Mount the source read-only and copy into a container-local scratch dir instead of writing back into $REPO; pin the base image by digest (see separate finding).

findings.title: Unpinned mutable base image tag (archlinux:latest) in the build container
evidence: live/ci-build.sh:62 - 'archlinux:latest' used as the build environment with no digest pin
live/ci-build.sh:71 - pacman -Sy --noconfirm then installs archiso/dosfstools/python into that mutable base
findings.impact: The exact build environment is not reproducible and can change without any repo change: a new 'latest' image or an upstream pacman state can alter or compromise the ISO build silently, and there is no digest recorded to audit what was actually built.
findings.recommendation: Pin the base image by digest (e.g. archlinux@sha256:...) in live/ci-build.sh, or publish a controlled builder image and reference its digest; record the digest in the build log/artifact metadata. Combine with the least-privilege change above.

findings.title: bench-agent service runs unsandboxed with no runtime hardening profile while executing control-plane shell commands
evidence: server/bench-agent.service:1-17 - no User=, NoNewPrivileges, ProtectSystem, PrivateTmp, CapabilityBoundingSet or SystemCallFilter; runs as root by default
AGENTS.md:185-186 - 'The remote exec command is a real shell on the runner - it's gated by the operator token; treat it as privileged'
bench/agent.py:273-274,319-324 - the agent handles 'exec'/'shell' by calling run_exec(...)
bench/benchreport.py:811 - def run_exec(reporter, cmd, timeout=120, cwd=None) is the raw command runner
server/benchd.service:14-18 - by contrast benchd ships NoNewPrivileges/PrivateTmp/ProtectSystem/ProtectHome; the agent that actually executes commands has none
findings.impact: The service that executes operator-supplied shell commands has no container-like confinement (no capability dropping, no filesystem/namespace restrictions), so any compromise of the control-plane token or the agent loop yields unconstrained root on the benchmark host. This is the runtime-hardening gap the domain asks to profile.
findings.recommendation: Add a systemd hardening block to server/bench-agent.service: User=/DynamicUser where feasible, NoNewPrivileges=true, ProtectSystem=strict + ReadWritePaths for the results/work dirs, ProtectHome, PrivateTmp, PrivateDevices (GPU paths need /dev/nvidia* so scope carefully), ProtectKernelTunables/Modules, RestrictSUIDSGID, SystemCallFilter=@system-service, and a CapabilityBoundingSet=~. Run exec jobs in a dedicated, least-privilege worker. Mirror the same profile for the live-USB units.

findings.title: LXC deployment binds the control plane to 0.0.0.0 despite documented 'LAN/lab address only' posture
evidence: server/benchd.service:11 - ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /opt/bench-test/server/benchd.py --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8722
docs/CONTROL_PLANE.md:208-209 - 'Bind to the LAN/lab address only. On the lab overlay it is reachable over the wgaudit0 WireGuard network'
docs/CONTROL_PLANE.md:170-185 - the documented deployment is an unprivileged LXC ('--unprivileged 1') running this unit
server/benchd.py:1439-1440 - at startup it logs 'OPEN (no token)' when no token is configured
findings.impact: The shipped unit (and the LXC deploy recipe) exposes the control plane on every interface, contradicting the documented LAN-only intent; in an LXC with bridged networking this can reach networks beyond the lab. Combined with the no-token 'OPEN' mode, a misconfigured deploy is remotely reachable.
findings.recommendation: Have the unit bind the documented lab address (or make host configurable via /etc/benchd.conf and default to the overlay address), or add a firewall rule. Document that the 0.0.0.0 bind is intentional only when a host firewall/reverse proxy constrains it; refuse to start when no token is set.
